actions.justification: Essential first step in ADHF evaluation to confirm volume overload (wet state) based on JVD, peripheral edema, pulmonary crackles — guides diuretic therapy.

Critical to differentiate warm vs. cold profile. Patient's BP is 145/88 suggesting warm profile, but must confirm adequate perfusion before selecting therapy (warm-wet vs. cold-wet changes treatment).
BNP quantifies degree of heart failure decompensation, confirms ADHF diagnosis, and provides baseline for monitoring treatment response.
Patient is warm and wet (elevated BP, congestion, SpO2 90%, dyspnea/orthopnea). IV loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) is first-line therapy for ADHF with volume overload per AHA guidelines.
Chest X-ray is essential to confirm pulmonary edema, assess degree of congestion, and rule out other causes of dyspnea (pneumonia, pleural effusion).
BMP needed to assess renal function and electrolytes before and after diuresis, particularly important in HFrEF patients who may have renal impairment or electrolyte abnormalities.
Order troponin to evaluate for ACS as a precipitant of ADHF decompensation. This is a key diagnostic step in the workup of acute decompensated heart failure.

Patient has elevated BP (145/88) with warm-wet ADHF profile. Vasodilator therapy (e.g., IV nitroglycerin) reduces preload and afterload, improving dyspnea and pulmonary congestion. Not contraindicated in this warm-wet presentation.
Patient has known HFrEF with atrial fibrillation presenting with ADHF decompensation. Cardiology input is needed for optimization of GDMT, rate control strategy, and further management guidance.

Echocardiography is indicated to assess current LV function, wall motion, and hemodynamic status in this patient with HFrEF presenting with ADHF. It will help differentiate warm-wet vs cold-wet profile and guide further management, especially given SpO2 of 90% and elevated BP.

While the patient currently appears warm-wet (elevated BP, MAP 107), ongoing assessment for cardiogenic shock or low-output state is warranted. If perfusion reassessment (cold profile) is confirmed, inotrope initiation would be appropriate. This action is conditionally triggered based on hemodynamic profile.
Mandatory action not yet completed. Obtain detailed history of HF exacerbation including triggers, medication compliance, dietary indiscretion, and prior HF history to guide management.
Mandatory action not yet completed. Physical exam is critical to assess volume status (JVD, edema, rales), perfusion (skin temp, cap refill), and hemodynamic profile in ADHF.
Mandatory action not yet completed. ECG required to evaluate rate control in known atrial fibrillation, identify ischemia as precipitant, and assess for arrhythmia contributing to decompensation.

Mandatory action per ADHF workup guideline. CBC is needed to evaluate for anemia (which can exacerbate heart failure and dyspnea), infection, or other hematologic contributors. Not previously completed under this action_id.

Mandatory action per ADHF workup guideline. TSH is needed to rule out thyroid dysfunction (hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism) as a precipitant of acute decompensated heart failure, especially given the atrial fibrillation comorbidity.

Patient has SpO2 90% and elevated BP 145/88 with tachycardia, suggesting a 'warm and wet' hemodynamic profile (ADHF). Formal hemodynamic profile assessment will guide appropriate treatment selection (vasodilators vs diuretics vs other interventions) and avoid contraindicated therapies.
Mandatory action per protocol. BMP needed to assess renal function, electrolytes, and guide diuretic dosing in ADHF. Must be completed despite 85-minute mark.
Mandatory action per protocol. BNP/NT-proBNP quantifies degree of cardiac stress and guides ADHF management and prognosis.
Mandatory action per protocol. Chest X-ray assesses pulmonary congestion severity, pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly in this dyspneic ADHF patient with SpO2 90%.
Patient is hypertensive (BP 145/88, MAP 107) with ADHF. Adding a vasodilator can reduce afterload, improve cardiac output, and relieve congestion in the warm-wet profile.
Patient has signs of volume overload (orthopnea, weight gain, SpO2 90%, RR 26). Augmenting diuresis is indicated for congestion relief per AHA HF guidelines.
Patient has HFrEF with AF; reassessing LVEF helps guide GDMT optimization and device therapy decisions. Echo was ordered but LVEF assessment should be explicitly documented.

NYHA functional class assessment is essential for guiding further management decisions, including GDMT optimization, device therapy candidacy (ICD/CRT), and discharge planning in this HFrEF patient presenting with ADHF.

ICD assessment is indicated in HFrEF patients. Once the acute decompensation is stabilized, evaluating ICD candidacy per AHA guidelines is appropriate, especially given the underlying HFrEF and atrial fibrillation.
CRT assessment is warranted in HFrEF patients to determine if cardiac resynchronization therapy may improve symptoms and outcomes, particularly in those with reduced EF and potential dyssynchrony.
Patient has SpO2 of 90% and RR of 26 with significant dyspnea despite initial treatment. ICU admission is warranted for close monitoring and potential escalation of therapy.
